title: Bringing Ideas Home to Ogden Valley: Lessons, partnerships, and opportunities from the Utah League of Cities and Towns Conference
author: Mayor Janet Wampler
paragraphs: Last week, I had the opportunity to attend the Utah League of Cities and Towns (ULCT) Annual Conference in Salt Lake City. In keeping with my commitment to fiscal responsibility, I applied for and received a ULCT scholarship that covered both the conference registration and related travel expenses. That means our city received valuable training, education, and networking opportunities at no additional cost to local taxpayers.

Over two days, I participated in 10 workshops and meetings, along with several networking events, covering topics that directly impact rural communities like ours. I returned with new ideas, new contacts, and a deeper understanding of the challenges and opportunities facing municipalities across Utah.

One of the conference's keynote speakers was Frank Abagnale, a nationally recognized expert on fraud and identity theft. His presentation focused on how artificial intelligence is making scams more sophisticated and more difficult to detect. He emphasized that seniors continue to be among the most heavily targeted victims. The information was eye-opening, and in the coming weeks I will be sharing some of his recommendations through a series of articles focused on protecting our residents, families, and local government from emerging fraud threats.

Economic development was another major focus. During a workshop on strengthening rural economies, representatives from the Governor's Office of Economic Opportunity, USDA, and the Utah Small Business Credit Initiative discussed state and federal grants available to rural communities and small businesses. We also received advance information on new programs being developed to support entrepreneurship, startup businesses, and AI training for local companies. The availability of additional low-interest loan programs for rural businesses was particularly encouraging. Watch for future OVN articles that will help connect local entrepreneurs and business owners with these opportunities.

One session that particularly resonated with me focused on Utah's aging population and the steps communities can take to help seniors remain active, independent, and engaged. We reviewed examples from other Utah cities that have intentionally incorporated senior-friendly policies into their planning efforts. Representatives from AARP also shared information about grants available for accessibility improvements and senior-focused community projects.

This workshop reinforced my belief that our community would benefit from the creation of a Senior Advisory Group. Such a group could provide valuable input to Council as we look for ways to ensure residents can comfortably "age in place" while continuing to enjoy all that makes Ogden Valley special. If this is something you would like to see pursued, I encourage you to reach out to your Council representative.

Another topic that continues to generate interest statewide is Advanced Air Mobility (AAM). While some have associated this technology with the upcoming Olympics, state officials made it clear that AAM is not being developed for the Olympics. Rather, the Olympics happen to align with the anticipated timeline for implementation. Utah remains firmly committed to integrating this emerging technology into the state's transportation system, and I learned that Ogden Valley has been identified as a community of interest in future planning discussions. This is a topic residents will likely hear more about in Council meetings and future articles.

Equally valuable was the opportunity to meet with mayors and elected officials from rural communities throughout Utah. We discussed common challenges, exchanged ideas, and shared lessons learned. I left with more than a dozen new contacts who can serve as resources as we continue addressing the issues facing our community. Sometimes one of the greatest benefits of these conferences is simply learning from the experiences of others who have already tackled problems similar to our own.

Additional sessions covered state policy issues, transportation planning, energy, infrastructure financing, downtown revitalization, and effective conflict resolution. One workshop featured communities that have successfully revitalized their downtown districts, creating inviting public spaces while supporting local businesses. Another focused on practical skills for navigating disagreements and maintaining productive conversations in close-knit communities. In today's environment, those may be some of the most important leadership skills we can develop.

A recurring theme throughout the conference was the importance of long-term planning. Whether discussing transportation, infrastructure, economic development, or services for seniors, successful communities are thinking years ahead rather than simply reacting to immediate challenges. The knowledge gained at this conference will help inform Council discussions and future planning efforts as we continue working to preserve the character of our valley while preparing thoughtfully for the future.

Most importantly, thanks to the scholarship provided by ULCT, our city was able to benefit from these educational opportunities without adding any cost to taxpayers. I appreciate the investment that organizations like ULCT make in local government leaders, and I look forward to sharing what I learned with both Council and the residents we serve.
As always, thank you for your continued engagement, your feedback, and your commitment to making Ogden Valley an exceptional place to call home.
